title: 'I'll Come Home Next Diwali': The Kargil Officer's Promise That Stayed Unkept
excerpt: Captain Amit Bhardwaj, 27, of 4 JAT volunteered to search for Captain Saurabh Kalia's missing patrol on May 17, 1999, and held off infiltrators at Kaksar so his men could withdraw. His body came home 57 days later.
body:
• Captain Amit Bhardwaj of the 4 JAT Regiment was killed on May 17, 1999, in the Kaksar sector during the Kargil War, after volunteering to search for Captain Saurabh Kalia's missing patrol, family and regimental accounts say.
  • He gave covering fire so his men could pull back; his body was recovered 57 days later, on July 13, 1999, with his weapon still in his hand.
  • The Times of India, retelling his story this Diwali, records the promise at its heart: he told his mother he would come home next Diwali. The war intervened first.
  • His sister Sunita Dhonkaria runs the Shaheed Amit Bhardwaj Memorial Trust, founded in September 1999; the bridge at Kaksar has been renamed Capt. Amit Bhardwaj Setu.

He told his mother he would come home next Diwali. That is the promise The Times of India placed at the centre of its Diwali retelling of Captain Amit Bhardwaj's story — a 27-year-old officer from Jaipur who did not come home, because the Kargil War came first. Twenty-seven Diwalis later, the story is still told in his family in the present tense.

Jaipur to Kaksar

Amit Bhardwaj was born on March 4, 1972, the only child of O.P. Sharma and Sushila Sharma of Jaipur. He graduated from Rajasthan University, joined the Army in 1997 and was commissioned into the 4 JAT Regiment. After a first tenure at Pithoragarh, he was posted to the Kaksar area of Kargil. His sister Sunita Dhonkaria, writing about him, records that he confided only to the family doctor that the Army was his destination — he had chosen it over the doctor-or-engineer path set out for him.

May 17, 1999

When a patrol of six soldiers led by Captain Saurabh Kalia went missing, Bhardwaj volunteered to find them. "Saurabh is my junior, it's my duty to find him and his team," his sister recalls him saying. On May 17, 1999, he led a search party into the Kaksar sector. At Bajrang Post the party came under enemy fire. Bhardwaj held position and gave covering fire while his men withdrew — soldiers who were there told his mother afterwards that his stand is why the unit learned the enemy had taken posts inside Indian territory, and why men who would otherwise have been killed got out. Accounts of the action credit him with killing more than ten infiltrators. His body could not be brought back; it was recovered on July 13, 1999, 57 days after his death, his weapon still in his hand. The family, his sister writes, was told only after 56 days that he had been killed.

"Had Amit not given cover fire to his men, all would have been killed in action, and we would not have known that the enemy had captured a few of our posts."

— Jatveer, the Jat Regiment magazine, as quoted by his sister Sunita Dhonkaria

What carries his name now

His last rites were performed at Malviya Nagar Park in Jaipur, where the government has built his memorial. The family formed the Shaheed Amit Bhardwaj Memorial Charitable Trust in September 1999, which runs plantation drives, blood donation camps and support for poor students, according to his sister's account. The bridge at Kaksar, the sector where he died, has been renamed Capt. Amit Bhardwaj Setu, with a memorial inaugurated by his sister.

The Diwali frame is the family's, not an editor's invention: a festival of homecoming, and a son whose leave never came. The Times of India's account is a reminder that for some households the festival's central story — the return home — is the one that stayed unfinished in 1999.
